title: Ovary
description: Female reproductive organ that produces egg cells
wiki_lead:
The ovary (from Latin  ōvārium 'egg') is the paired primary sex organ, or gonad in the female reproductive system. The ovaries are responsible for the production of oogonia, their development to oocytes (immature egg cells), and the release as a mature egg cell (ovum) at ovulation. The egg cells, or ova are also known as gametes, and the process of their development is gametogenesis, known as oogenesis in the female. During their development each oocyte is surrounded by granulosa cells, forming an ovarian follicle. The ovary progresses through many stages beginning in the prenatal period through menopause.
The ovary also produces hormones, specifically sex hormones (sex steroids) to assist in the development of the egg cells. This hormone production in the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles,  makes the ovary an endocrine gland as well as a sex organ. The hormones are estrogen, and progesterone that also play an important part in the development and function of the female reproductive organs, and in  the development at puberty of secondary sex characteristics.
The paired ovaries are located one on either side of the uterus, and connect with the uterus through the fallopian tubes. They are held in place by the ovarian ligament, and the suspensory ligament of the ovary.
Many of the structural and functional features of the human ovary are shared with other mammals and vertebrates and ovaries of some kind are found in many invertebrates. This article is primarily about the human ovary.

Structure
At puberty each ovary measures around  3 cm in length by 1.5 cm wide and is 1 cm thick, and sits in a depression in the lateral wall of the pelvic cavity. This depression is called the ovarian fossa and measures around 4 cm x 3 cm x 2 cm. The fossa is bounded above by the external iliac artery and vein, in front by the obliterated umbilical artery, and behind by the ureter. 
The ovaries lie within the peritoneal cavity on either side of the uterus to which they are attached via a fibrous cord called the ovarian ligament. They are tethered to the body wall via the suspensory ligament of the ovary, which is a posterior extension of the broad ligament of the uterus. The part of the broad ligament of the uterus that suspends the ovary is known as the mesovarium.
The ovary has an inner medullary core, and an outer cortical region, and is enclosed by a capsule of dense fibrous tissue the tunica albuginea. A layer of cuboidal epithelium from the visceral peritoneum covers the ovaries as ovarian surface epithelium.
The ovarian medulla  is the highly vascular stromal tissue in the center of the ovary.  Its contents include blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, immune cells, and nerves. 
The ovarian hilum is the hilum in the ovary, formed by  the stroma and attached to the ovarian ligament where the blood vessels, lymphatic vessels  and nerves enter the medulla of the ovary.
It is also the main site of ovarian hilus cells also known as ovarian ovarian Leydig cells.
The ovarian cortex is an ill-defined outer region containing many ovarian follicles at different stages of development. The follicles are surrounded by peripheral  stroma. It can be hard to distinguish between the cortex and medulla, but follicles are usually not found in the medulla.


Rete ovarii

The rete ovarii is an epithelial appendage of the ovary to which it is attached. It has been proposed to be presented as an ovarian organ. Before advanced imaging techniques were available the rete ovarii was overlooked as an insignificant embryonic remnant. It has been shown to be a structure of three distinct regions. Columnar epithelial cells create a tubular region ending in blind tips termed the extraovarian rete (EOR). Pseudocolumnar epithelial cells make up a connecting rete (CR). And squamous epithelial cells branch into an intricate network of thin cords of cells with a diameter of around 1-3 cells, known as the intraovarian rete (IOR). The CR connects the EOR to the IOR. grok_lead: The ovary is one of a pair of almond-shaped female gonads located in the pelvic cavity, serving as the primary reproductive organs responsible for producing ova (eggs) and secreting key hormones that regulate the menstrual cycle, fertility, and secondary sexual characteristics. In human anatomy, each ovary measures approximately 3.5 cm in length, 2 cm in width, and 1 cm in thickness, resembling a large olive, and is positioned in the ovarian fossa on either side of the uterus within the broad ligament of the peritoneum. The organ consists of an outer cortex containing ovarian folliclesâstructures that house developing oocytesâand an inner medulla composed of loose connective tissue, blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves, all enclosed by a thin germinal epithelium and a fibrous tunica albuginea capsule. The ovaries are suspended by peritoneal ligaments, including the ovarian ligament and suspensory ligament, which also facilitate their connection to the fallopian tubes for ovum transport during ovulation. Functionally, the ovaries play a central role in oogenesis, the process of egg maturation, where primordial follicles develop monthly under hormonal influence, culminating in the release of a mature oocyte during ovulation triggered by a luteinizing hormone surge. They also function as endocrine glands, primarily producing estrogen (from granulosa cells in follicles) and progesterone (from the corpus luteum post- ovulation), with smaller amounts of testosterone and inhibin, all regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis to maintain reproductive health and influence traits such as breast development, body shape, and bone density. Throughout a woman's life, ovarian function evolves: the pool of primordial follicles reaches its maximum during fetal development and subsequently declines throughout life, ovulation occurs cyclically from puberty to menopause, and post- menopause, the ovaries atrophy, reducing hormone output and increasing risks for conditions like osteoporosis.
